1.title: System Prompts, Templates and Prompting Techniques
1.text: Welcome to Module five: System Prompts, Templates and Prompting Techniques. This module covers system prompts, templates and prompting techniques. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The anatomy of a system prompt and what belongs in it. Templates: stable text plus variable slots. Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought and when each helps. Guardrail prompts and their limits. How to treat prompts as versioned, tested artifacts.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Writes the System Prompt for a Bank's Policy Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Writes the System Prompt for a Bank's Policy Assistant. The assistant answers staff questions from a policy library. It must cite sources, say when policy is silent, refuse legal advice, and answer in a fixed Jason (Java Script Object Notation) shape for the agent desktop.

1.title: System Prompts
1.text: System Prompts. The figure shows this: Anatomy of a system prompt: role and purpose, audience, rules and boundaries, tone and format, how to use sources, uncertainty and refusal behavior, output schema.

1.title: System Prompts, continued
1.text: System Prompts, continued. Role and purpose. Write: Who the model is and the job. Example: "You answer staff questions about retail-banking policy". Audience. Write: Who reads the output. Example: "Contact-center agents, not customers". Rules and boundaries. Write: Must and must-not, with the reason. Example: "Never give legal advice: staff cannot rely on it with customers". Sources. Write: How to use the context. Example: "Use only the provided policy excerpts; quote the clause". Uncertainty. Write: What to do when unsure. Example: "If the excerpts do not cover it, say so and suggest escalation". Format. Write: Structure, length, schema. Example: "Return Jason with fields answer, citations, confidence".

1.title: System Prompts, continued
1.text: System Prompts, continued. Be clear and direct: Claude is a brilliant new employee with no context; state the task, the constraints and why. Put long documents first and the question and instructions last; separate content with X M L-style tags ( less than policy greater than, less than question greater than ). A role sentence focuses tone and behavior. Hard requirements belong in code (validation, permissions), with the prompt as the first layer, not the only one (Module thirteen).

1.title: Templates and Reuse
1.text: Templates and Reuse. A template holds stable instructions and named variable slots (user input, retrieved passages, customer tier). Stable parts first, variable parts last: this keeps a cacheable prefix (Module six). Separate data from instructions with tags so injected text is treated as data. Keep prompts in version control, with tests (evals) and a change log; roll back when quality drops. Modular prompts: shared blocks (tone, safety rules) reused across assistants; per-use blocks (task, schema). Exam tip: Templates put the static content first and the dynamic content last. That ordering is also what makes prompt caching work.

1.title: Prompting Techniques
1.text: Prompting Techniques. The figure shows this: Three techniques: zero-shot with instructions only, few-shot with labeled examples, and chain-of-thought with reasoning before the answer.

1.title: Prompting Techniques, continued
1.text: Prompting Techniques, continued. Zero-shot. What it is: Instructions only, no examples. Use when: Clear, common tasks; strong models. Watch for: Format drift on unusual outputs. Few-shot. What it is: three to five relevant, diverse examples in tags. Use when: Steering format, tone, edge cases; classification boundaries. Watch for: Examples that are too similar bias the output; keep them in an examples block, not instructions. Chain-of-thought. What it is: Ask for step-by-step reasoning before the answer. Use when: Multi-step reasoning, math, analysis, checks. Watch for: Extra tokens and latency; with thinking models prefer effort and adaptive thinking over manual step prompts.

1.title: Prompting Techniques, continued
1.text: Prompting Techniques, continued. Self-check or critique. What it is: Ask the model to review a draft against criteria. Use when: Quality pass before output. Watch for: Not a replacement for external validation. Prompt chaining. What it is: Separate calls for stages. Use when: Complex tasks needing inspection. Watch for: Latency. Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer structure and tone; they must be relevant, diverse and clearly marked. Structured outputs (schema-constrained decoding) enforce shape; they do not guarantee truth (validate values). To reduce hallucination: allow "I don't know", ask for direct quotes before conclusions, require citations, and ground in provided sources.

1.title: Prompting Techniques, continued
1.text: Prompting Techniques, continued. Test prompts on a dataset, not on a few hand-picked examples.

1.title: Guardrails in Prompts
1.text: Guardrails in Prompts. Scope statement. Purpose: Keep the assistant on topic. Limits: Users can still try to override. Refusal rules with reasons. Purpose: Stop prohibited help. Limits: Not enforceable alone. Source-grounding rules. Purpose: Reduce invention. Limits: Still needs verification. Untrusted-content notice. Purpose: Treat tool and document text as data. Limits: Pair with isolation and least privilege. Output format and schema. Purpose: Predictable downstream use. Limits: Shape only. Prompt guardrails are the first layer. Enforcement (hooks, validation, authorization, human approval) is in code (Module thirteen). Exam tip: Prompts are soft controls: they guide behavior but cannot enforce a hard rule, so pair them with code. Exam tip: Few-shot examples steer format and tone best; chain-of-thought helps multi-step reasoning at the price of tokens.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. System prompt: Role, audience, rules with reasons, sources, uncertainty, format. Order: Long documents and stable text first; question and variables last. Template: Stable text plus variable slots; tags separate data from instructions. Few-shot: three to five relevant, diverse, tagged examples. Co T: For multi-step reasoning; costs tokens; use effort and thinking on thinking models. Hallucination: Allow abstaining, quote first, cite, ground. Schema: Shape not truth: validate values. Prompts as code: Version, test with evals, roll back.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A prompt template places the user's question first, followed by a six thousand-token policy that is identical on every request. Latency and cost are both concerns. What change helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A stable prefix can be cached only if it comes first and does not change.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An assistant must output labeled risk levels in a house style that is hard to describe. Which technique fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Examples are the most reliable way to convey format and tone.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Why should instructions in a system prompt include the reason for a rule? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Explaining the why lets Claude generalize the intent.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A schema-constrained output returns well-formed Jason with a wrong account balance. What does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A schema guarantees the shape of the output but not the truth of its values, so content must be validated against the source.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two reduce hallucination in a document-grounded assistant? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Permission to abstain and quote-first grounding make unsupported claims visible.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. When is chain-of-thought prompting most useful? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Step-by-step reasoning helps complex tasks and costs extra tokens.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which statement about prompt guardrails is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Prompts can be overridden; enforce critical rules outside the model.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: C. Question five: D and E. Question six: D. Question seven: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
